I once hired a developer who came highly recommended. I was told he was exceptionally talented, worked fast, and delivered excellent results. There was one warning: he rarely stayed in one place for more than a few weeks. I hired him anyway. From his first days on the project, he moved development forward at a pace I had never seen. A few days in, I asked him to show me where things stood. He was almost done. There was just one small problem: he had built something else. Press enter or click to view image in full size An impressive solution can be a long way from the right assignment. AI-generated illustration. It was not bad work. Quite the opposite. If we had needed what he built, it could have been an excellent solution. But we had no demand for it. He had nearly crossed into a different domain from the one I had hired him to work in. We sat down and talked. I explained what we were trying to achieve, who needed the solution, and what was missing from what he had built. He understood, changed course, and adapted his work to the actual need. He did that at remarkable speed too. That was when I understood who I was working with: a galloping horse. If I slowed him down at every step, I would lose the very quality that had brought him to the team. If I let him disappear over the horizon without checking where he was going, I might again receive a brilliant creation that we could not use. So I let him run. I set the direction and checked along the way that he was still moving toward it. What followed was a period of remarkable output and ingenuity. He stayed on my team for two years. When he left, both he and the friend who had recommended him said that staying so long in one place was unusual for him. Freedom Was Part of the Method Since then, I have looked for people like him: people who bring energy, dive into a problem, and see possibilities before anyone else has noticed them. They are especially valuable when a task calls for invention, experimentation, and bold thinking. But not every task calls for a sprint, and not everyone works the same way. Some people excel at steady, methodical, precise work. Leading a good team means knowing its people, matching work to their strengths, and giving each of them enough room to do their best work. This is the approach I developed: I set the direction, give considerable freedom in how to get there, and check during execution that the work is still heading toward the goal. I did not assign someone to inspect his every step. Nor did I wait until the end to see where he had arrived. The faster he moved, the more frequently I needed to check for drift. Now I Work With a Different Kind of Galloping Horse Today I use the same approach with an AI agent. I describe a task and new possibilities appear almost immediately: another solution, an extension, a direction worth exploring. Sometimes it builds something I could not have produced at that pace any other way. Sometimes, if I have not been clear enough, it races toward a problem I never asked it to solve. Of course, this is not the same relationship. A person has aspirations, judgment, a life outside work, and the right to leave. An AI agent has no motivation in the human sense, even when its behavior looks like eagerness to help. I do not have to worry that it will look for another job. I do have to make sure its speed and availability do not tempt me to skip the guidance I would give a human teammate. Before it starts running, I work with it to define the problem, the outcome I need, and the boundaries of the task. Then I ask it to tell me what it understood: what already exists in the system, what it plans to change, and what it will leave alone. If it is veering off course, we can correct that in a short conversation. After hours of work, the same mistake may look like an entire system. Then I let it work. I do not dictate every line of code or tug on the reins at every turn. I check progress in short stages, look at what it has built, and make sure it still serves the need we started with. A small, reversible task allows more freedom. When the work affects data, money, permissions, or a decision that is hard to undo, I set firmer boundaries and stop sooner. Choosing the right tool is part of the job too. Some models tend to propose and expand. Others are better suited, in my experience, to working carefully within a defined scope. I learn how each behaves in practice and choose according to the task. That resembles getting to know teammates with different working styles, even though the reasons for those differences are entirely different. The Risk Is Not Just a Crash What surprised me when I first checked on that developer was not that he had failed. He had nearly succeeded. He had built something good, quickly and confidently.
